utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Sorry, I've got a problem with my chair. I'm not beginning to run mad. I believe that the Prosecution has got some housekeeping to discuss before we call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Very briefly, Your Honour. The first thing is that according to the Trial Chamber's decision of the 30th of September, 2006, we are -- the Prosecution is supposed to file by Wednesday its response to the Defence submissions regarding the testimony of Milan Babic. And I would just like to request a few extra days to file our response and ask that we be allowed to file it on Monday, the 16th of October. I've checked with the Defence, and the Defence assents to this request. The reason for the request is simply the press of business. I just have a lot to do, and it falls on me to do this particular response, because I was the one who handled Milan Babic's testimony, and I'm just -- just preparing for witnesses and other matters, it just would be convenient for me to have until Monday, the 16th of October, to respond. I would also note that we had at some point asked to have an -- and have been granted a period of 10 days to respond to the Defence submission. When the original -- at some point when the schedule was set up, we had been given 10 days to respond, and then in the last decision, we asked again for that 10 days and it was interpreted by the Trial Chamber to be a request for an extension, when in fact we had just intended it to maintain the 10 days that had been originally granted to us and then we were granted only seven days. So what we're asking for is what we at some point had, but in any event I'm just asking, because it would be more convenient. Thank you. I have two other matters, if you want -- I don't know if the Trial Chamber wants to decide on that, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the Trial Chamber deal with this one first while it still remembers the damage done to your argument by the last couple of sentences on that first point. Mr. Milovancevic, do you confirm the Defence's agreement to this request? Good afternoon to you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. We agree, fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We confirm that the last couple of sentences of your argument undermined your application, but nonetheless, it persuades me to agree. So that the extension is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Thank you, Your Honour. The only other two issues are the Defence has filed a motion for protective measures for the next witness, MM-117. It was filed, I believe, today. I don't know if the Trial Chamber has received it but we just received it. But in any event, we have no opposition to the motion, just so the Trial Chamber is aware of our position. We do not oppose the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say "the next witness," the witness we are about to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, the witness after that, the witness that will start either tomorrow or the next day. Probably the next day, I would think. MM-117.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic? You have filed -- I haven't seen the motion. I don't know, maybe my brother and sister may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I received information from the Defence team that this has been submitted in the course of this morning. Yesterday, in our contacts with the witness, we established the need for these measures, which is why we only did this today, and my learned friend Mr. Whiting is right in saying that this is the witness who will be called after the next witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I hear what you say, but I would imagine that at some stage in the past when the Trial Chamber asked if you could make this application -- encompass an application for all witnesses you intend calling so that it could be dealt with in one application, I don't know whether it's for protective measures or it was for safe conduct, but some kind of request had been made to that effect and I think it would be appropriate for both types of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in principle, I fully agree with Your Honour's position. However, with each particular witness, specific circumstances sometimes arise. The first application or the first motion was for safe conduct. This witness, however, is now asking for protective measures, and I only learned that yesterday evening. That is why the motion was submitted so late. There is no other reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But you say you have no objections? Okay. The Chamber will deal with the motion when it becomes aware of it. Next point, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And actually, on that last point, I would fully agree with Mr. Milovancevic, and it happened to us, that witnesses often say at the last minute reasons for protective measures. On the -- the third point I wanted to raise is, had to do with 92 bis or 92 quater, formally 89(F) witnesses. We had -- we had understood that we were going to receive a motion last week on the 2nd of October with respect to the first batch. I've had communications with the Defence, not with Mr. Milovancevic himself but with Mr. Sekulic, and apparently on the Defence side, there was a mis -- I don't want to speak for them, but apparently there was a misunderstanding and they thought it was today that it was supposed to be filed, even though they agreed that on the record it's clear that it was supposed to be -- that it was October 2nd. In any event, it hasn't been filed and it's become a little pressing, because we've just received the list of the next group of witnesses that will testify after the four that we knew about already, and this group of six will probably start sometime next week. Of the six that are listed, four of them are supposed to testify via 89(F), 92 quater, and we have not received a motion or the statement or anything. And if they're going to testify next week, it makes -- it makes it extremely hard to prepare and also for us to respond to the motion for the Trial Chamber to consider it for all this to get done, so it's now very late for this all to happen. So I just wanted to raise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether my learned friend, Mr. Whiting, has properly understood our submission and I will check this during the first break. It would be completely unacceptable for us to bring the Prosecutor into a position where four witnesses are to be called and he has not yet received the 92 bis materials. We are working on these materials, and we will do our very best to adopt a rhythm which is completely acceptable to the OTP, because of course they cannot receive a statement today for a witness to appear tomorrow. The witnesses will be viva voce witnesses but please allow me to check this after the first break, or during the first break, and then after the first break I will be in a situation to give you the right information. And if I may add, we have been working on this intensively. We have had a problem that had to do with the on-site visit. Our investigator was in The Hague from the 21st to the 29th of September, which means he was not in Belgrade and was not able to be in contact with the witnesses who will testify under these Rules. It was only after the on-site visit that we were able to begin organising this part of our activities. So we would not wish Your Honours or our learned friends to think we had neglected to do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have a response to that, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy to take it up again after the first break, when Mr. Milovancevic has had a chance to look at it. But I would like to take it up, because I don't believe I've misunderstood, and I think we're already in a difficult position from the point of view of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. We will take it up after the first break, Mr. Milovancevic. Make sure you double-check and if indeed there are four witnesses who are 92 bis or 92 quater -- how do you pronounce that word?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no idea. I think it is -- I'm not even going to try. I'm not even going to try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Please make sure that then if we have those 92 bis or something, something, witnesses, let's get the statements. Okay. Is that all? Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic, any housekeeping? Any housekeeping matter on your side?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at present, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Next witness, Mr. Whiting -- Mr. Milovancevic, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have made the solemn declaration, and as of this moment the Defence will begin your examination-in-chief. The rules of these proceedings prescribe that during your testimony you cannot use any materials. I assume that you had -- you have these materials with you while preparing but please put them away now. Thank you very much. Before I ask you for personal details, I wish to make a request. I would like both of us to speak slowly and make pauses between question and answer, so that the interpreters can do their job. Would you please tell us your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Nikola Medakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When and where were you born, and what education do you have?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 1st of January, 1967, in Plaski, where I completed primary and the first two grades of secondary school, and then the third and fourth grade I completed in Ogulin. That was the mathematical secondary school. I then enrolled in the faculty of agriculture where I studied from 1986 to 1990, but I did not graduate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While we are discussing personal details, could you tell us what your ethnicity and religion is.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb and my religion is Orthodox, Christian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you reside after completing your education? I heard that you completed the secondary -- your secondary schooling in 1986.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: A correction. I completed it in 1985, and then under the then legislation, I did my military service in Zadar. Then I went to study in Zagreb and I visited my parents near Plaski, and this is where I was residing between 1990 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note they did not hear the name of the village near Plaski where the witness's parents lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Milovancevic. The interpreters did not hear the name of the village near Plaski, where the witness's parents lived, and I did not also hear the witness answer your question where he resides now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will get these answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, you mentioned a village near Plaski where you were born. Would you repeat the name of that village once more.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: It's called Medakovici, and Janja Gora 32 is the address.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In respect of the question of His Honour Judge Moloto, I asked you where you resided in 1990 and 1991. Did you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that at that time you resided in Plaski?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My house is about two and a half or three kilometres from the centre of Plaski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about your address, can you tell us where you reside today, and since when. I don't mean your address, but simply the area.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I've been living in Serbia since 1995. I'm currently in Sremski Karlovci; it's a small town near Novisad. I've been living there for the last three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say you resided in Plaski. What was the situation in Plaski up to 1990?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Plaski is a place with five or six -- or was a place with five or 6.000 inhabitants. It was a cluster of villages: Latin, Vojinovac, Plavca Draga, Licka Jesenica. And Saborsko was some 20 kilometres away in the direction of the Plitvice lakes. The seat of the municipality was in Ogulin. Ogulin municipality had about 30.000 inhabitants. The secondary schools were there. In Plaski most people were employed in the cellulose and paper factory, which employed about a thousand people. There were quite a few retired people there, too, and people who were farmers. I don't know what situation you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will put more questions to you about this. When you told us the number of people who lived in Plaski, can you tell us what their ethnic composition was?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: In Plaski itself and the surrounding villages, apart from Saborsko, 97 to 98 per cent perhaps were Serbs. There were a few mixed marriages, and during the war I happened to learn from the European Union mission, there were about 70 people who were not Serbs, in that area, in total. We never made these distinctions or counted people as to their ethnic affiliation. My sister-in-law is a Croat, for example, and that was never a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't draw these distinctions either, but I have to put questions that are relevant to this case. You say you lived in Plaski. You described the ethnic makeup of the population. What were inter-ethnic relations like up to 1990?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Up to 1990, when the HDZ won at the first multi-party elections, the situation was normal. Everybody went about their business. There were no inter-ethnic incidents, at least not any I know of, but I'm -- I don't think there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in 1990 the HDZ won the elections and that the situation was peaceful up to that point. What changes occurred then and what caused these changes? How did the way of life change?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I said that the people from Plaski - except for those who were employed in Plaski itself and that's about a thousand people working in the factory in Plaski - mostly went to work in the larger towns in Croatia, such as Rijeka, Zagreb, Ogulin. When the HDZ won the elections, people lost their jobs and came back to their family houses where their parents lived. Many of them lost their flats. So the number of residents in Plaski increased, whereas the number of people who had a job decreased. And then the factory stopped working, and every day we had problems with Croatian television, the media, provocations by Croats passing through Plaski. I'm referring primarily to the inhabitants of Saborsko. They held rallies in Ogulin, and in order for them to reach Ogulin, they had to travel through Plaski. While travelling through Plaski they displayed symbols which we found unacceptable because they reminded us of terrible events from our history, from World War II. I'm primarily referring to the chequer-board, as we called it, or the open display of the U symbol. Plaski itself and the surrounding area, when I say Plaski I mean to the -- I'm referring to the entire Plaski valley, two and a half to 3.000 people were killed by Ustasha in World War II. Not in any kind of fighting or offensive, but they were simply killed by the Ustasha, and the symbols used by the new Croatian authorities in 1990 were identical to the ones used during that pogrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your more extensive answer now, you just described the change in the situation. What was the reaction of the inhabitants in that area, in Plaski, and what was your personal reaction to those events, if there was any reaction at all?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: As we say, birds of feather flock together. When Croats started rallying around their national programme, the Serbs tried to organise themselves as well. That is to say, we in Plaski accepted the required idea of SAO Krajina. We organised a referendum, and the vast majority responded to the referendum. Over 99 per cent came out to vote, and they voted in this first Krajina referendum. Following that, we organised a referendum for local communes to step out of the Ogulin municipality, which had a majority of Croatian inhabitants, and the HDZ was the dominant party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Medakovic. If I can interrupt you. In that period of time, that is to say 1990, during the first multi-party elections, was there a political party that was founded in Plaski to which you perhaps belonged?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Plaski, in April, which is to say on the eve of multi-party elections, the SDS or democratic party was established. I think that it was in the eleventh hour that they managed to submit the paperwork for one candidate, which was Dimitrijev Kosanovic, and he was an assemblyman representing the SDS in Ogulin municipality. There were several other SDS -- I'm sorry, there were several other Serbs as assemblymen but they were representatives of other political parties, such as SDP and so on. But to answer your question, yes, the SDS was established in April of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us were you a member of that party?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was. I was a member of the SDS from its inception and my first duty was that of a secretary of a local board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned a referendum of sorts in Plaski. Can you tell us something in greater detail about it, why was there a referendum and why was it on this break -- breaking apart?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were dissatisfied with this new HDZ rule. Rudolf Spehar became president of municipality and he was a hawk of the HDZ, which reminded us of the spectres of the past, and it was back in 1990 that he spoke of the independent state of Croatia, back then. The situation in Plaski itself was such that it mandated that we self-organise. There was an increase in the number of inhabitants, and we wanted to make sure that our economic organisation was feasible and that we protect ourselves from the fate suffered by our ancestors in Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the inhabitants of Plaski. You said there were five to 6.000 people, and you said that the numbers of inhabitants increased, especially in late 1990. Increased to which extent, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: If I could give an estimate, I would say it increased by 20 per cent, which is to say that about 1.000 of people came back to their parent's homes, people who previously resided in the Rijeka, Karlovac, Zadar and so on, and they returned home because life became unbearable for them in these big cities because they were jobless. There was persecution and so on. They felt safer in Plaski, both for their own lives and for their families. A fact just occurred to me. We had a small health clinic, health station during peacetime. And then all of a sudden -- and there were eight physicians, specialists in Plaski. 17 forestry engineers, a large number of forestry technicians, which were traditional occupations in our region. So these were people fully fit for work, and they had to return home to their parents, with their families, because they were jobless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. You mentioned that about 1.000 people came back because they lost their jobs. Do you know why they lost their jobs?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Based on conversations with these people. Based on talks I had with my own brother, who used to work in Brinje as a forestry expert, and this is a town with -- predominantly inhabited by Croats. So based on these conversations, I learned that they lost their jobs only because they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you said that back in 1990 you reacted by organising a referendum. What was the purpose of this referendum and who organised it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time I was president of local commune in Plaski. There was a set procedure as to how to elect boards and so on, and I was supposed to head a board as president of a local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. You say that at that time you were president of the local commune. Can you tell us what period of time it was, a month, a year?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to 1990, summertime. Summer months. But I can't be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that's quite sufficient. You as president of the local commune, you and others, what did you do about the referendum? What was the purpose of that referendum?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the Plaski local commune, there were other local communes, Latin, Komanovac [phoen], Plavca Draga and Licka Jesenica. All of us together, presidents of these local communes plus the board, we decided to schedule a referendum where we wanted our citizens to state their will as to the possibility of our local communes seceding from Ogulin municipality and annexing themselves to Titova Korenica municipality. At the time that municipality was still known as Tito's Korenica, or Titova Korenica, and at that time the decision was made to join the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. In accordance with the constitution and the law, was it possible to organise such a referendum and to initiate such an action in view of the Croatian legislation and constitution?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were several lawyers on the team preparing the referendum. I believe that at the time there was a law on civil initiatives, and I think that it was perfectly legal. It was perfectly in keeping with the then existing legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell us in which year that referendum was held and what was the result of that referendum.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is how it was: Late that year, late in 1990, we held a public forum, and we spoke about the reasons for scheduling the referendum. We asked for citizens' support. This public discussion was called -- was held in Plaski, in the so-called ZAVNOH centre. We held a meeting there, attended by 200, 250 people, and we abided by a set procedure. The initiative was accepted to organise a referendum. And then on 22nd or 23rd of December it was organised. I know this because the day following that I was arrested and taken to the police station in Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the 22nd of December, or on the 23rd of December, as you said, you organised this political meeting where you decided to hold a referendum. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's precisely how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you said that a day following that you were arrested and taken to Ogulin. Who arrested you and what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime early in the morning, at around 8.00, a police patrol came. I knew one of the policemen on the team, and they told me that I had to follow them, to go to Ogulin for an interview there. I got ready, I got into my car -- or, rather, I got into the car, and then some of my neighbours saw that. I joined them and then we travelled for half an hour to 45 minutes before we reached Ogulin, and then I was taken to the police station in Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what happened at the police station. Who questioned you and what took place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: There I was met by a man with the last name of Grozovic; I don't remember his first name. He was deputy chief. And Ante Vujovic was the chief. And across the table was Rudolf Spehar, president of municipality. Rudolph Spehar was the one who spoke the most. He threatened me. I don't think I need to mention the threats, but what it all boiled down to was what right I had to talk against Croatia, and what right I had to speak of seceding from Croatia. And I said that I was representing the people, that I was the president of the local commune, and I said that this was my political orientation. And as we talked, which lasted for about an hour and half or two hours, I could see they were anxious and that they kept leaving the room. And then all of a sudden they said, "We're all going to Plaski." In the meantime, in Plaski, near the branch police office, and in that branch police office there were about 10 to 12 policemen, all of a sudden a large number of people assembled there, people from Plaski and from neighbouring areas, all of them assembled in front of the branch police station asking that I be released, or else they would -- they would block the police station. I drove in the car with Grozovic to that place, and as we came down there was a bit of a slope, and as we were going down I could see that there were about 2.000 people assembled there. It was cold. It was December. And all of them were awaiting my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Plaski, was the situation resolved and was the referendum ultimately held?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I asked the citizens to disperse peacefully. I told them that I wasn't abused, at least not physically. I told them that we would negotiate, that our referendum would be held, and this is how it was ultimately. There were no incidents. Not a single window-pane was broken, there were no problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When was the referendum held and what was its result?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. I know that the vast majority, that is to say we abided by the voters' list which existed with the political parties, and over 90 per cent voted in favour, in favour of the question put at the referendum. That was in early 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in the referendum, in early 1991, the answer was: Yes, or they were in favour of it. But you have to tell us what the question was?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: For each local commune, there was a special ballot and on it the question was: Do you support the secession of local commune of Plaski from Ogulin municipality and its annexation to Tito's Korenica municipality? And the vast majority voted in favour of it, the vast majority meaning 99 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Following the referendum, what happened to Plaski? Were there any changes, political changes, in view of the results of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Following this decision taken at the referendum, we became part of Korenica municipality, but since it was quite far away from Plaski, some 60 kilometres, we decided to establish a conference of local communes, an association of local communes in keeping with the then existing legislation in order to resolve various day-to-day problems that the inhabitants had. So as a local commune we started negotiations with the Croatian side, especially concerning the work of the branch police office in Plaski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just check if everything is okay with Mr. Martic; whether he is warm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Martic says that everything is fine and he thanks you for your concern. He just started coughing, but then he had some water and now he is feeling fine. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The conference of local communes, can you tell us when it was founded, just give us roughly the period of time.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: This conference functioned even prior to that. It started functioning in late 1990, but it was officially proclaimed after the referendum in early 1991, either January or February. I think it was already in January that it was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that as the conference of local communes, in that capacity you talked to the Croatian side. Who did you talk to and when?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Following that event in Plaski, when these people assembled, because I had been arrested -- I had been taken into custody and taken to Ogulin, the Croatian side perceived me as a serious negotiator, because they could see that I had support of the people. I talked to Josip Boljkovac, among other people. At the time he was minister of the interior. Then there was Slavko Degoricija there who acted as a negotiator with the Serbs. And then of course with the chief in Ogulin, Ante Vujovic, and chief of police administration in Karlovac who was called Ivan Stajduhar. We talked on several occasions. At the time I and my team advocated that all disputes be resolved peacefully. We agreed that the police branch office in Plaski ought to continue functioning with 12 policemen in total, out of which eight were Serbs and four were Croats from Saborsko. If we take into account the ethnic makeup of Saborsko and local communes around that area, they represented some 10 to 12 per cent, but we even agreed for them to be represented in twice as large numbers, because we wanted to show goodwill. At the time they used the old insignia, which was the five-pointed red star. They were still not using any Croatian symbols at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when these political negotiations were held and when the agreement was reached. Can you tell us what season it was, summer -- rather, spring or summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: All of this took place in early 1991, and it functioned until the 31st of March. I remember that date quite well. This was functioning until the 31st of March. As for negotiations, they started immediately following my arrest, which is to say in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to what you told us about the police branch office, the municipal seat was in Ogulin. Was there a police station in Ogulin?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was called the "policijska stanica [phoen]," the police station in Ogulin, according to the new terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In Plaski, however, there was an office. That's the lowest organisational unit or a branch office of the police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It had not existed for some 10 years previously. Everything was in Ogulin. Only patrols would come by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As the persons you spoke to who were representatives of the Croatian government, you mentioned Mr. Boljkovac. What office did he hold at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: He was the minister of the interior of the Republic of Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Degoricija. What office did he hold?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I went to negotiate with him on one occasion in the Croatian parliament in Zagreb. He was some sort of envoy of theirs for negotiations with local Serb communities. I think that's what they called it. But he was a man trusted by the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you negotiated with those persons about solving the political situation and the problems of everyday life, and that you also discussed the establishing of the local police branch of office. These problems that you discussed in early 1991 with the Croatian side, the minister of the interior and Mr. Degoricija, did you reach agreements and were they implemented?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we implemented everything, the Serb policemen wore the old insignia, as did the Croats who were employed in the police station. They dealt only with public security. We had problems with crime, problems like those that exist everywhere, and there had to be policemen dealing with those problems. They dealt with those problems well, in a proper manner, and all this functioned well until the 30th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Medakovic, you are mentioning the 31st of March, 1991, yet again. What happened on that day that changed the situation in Plaski?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 31st of March, the Orthodox church was celebrating Palm Sunday, while the Catholic church was celebrating Easter. In Plaski people traditionally assembled on that day, and Jovan Raskovic was due to arrive and the delegation from Knin, as well as the bishop from Gornji Karlovac, Vladika Nikanor. This was the night before. But a strong police unit under the command of Josip Turkovic passed through in a bus. They cut off the communications. They set up a check-point, and we later learned they were supposed to secure the flank for the MUP attack on Plitvice. That was the day of the first serious armed conflict at Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So what do you know about that conflict? Who came into conflict with whom and what was the outcome?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the one hand, there were special MUP forces of Croatia; on the other side were members of their reserve and active duty police force of the Krajina police from Korenica and some volunteers who were preventing the passage of those policemen. The outcome was that the special purpose policemen and the hotels in Plitvice and the JNA set up a buffer zone, to describe it very briefly. But throughout that day there were serious fighting and the man, I think he was called Rajko Vukadinovic from Korenica was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that someone on the Croatian side was killed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think there must be a mistake here. I said Vukadinovic. Rajko, Rajko Vukadinovic. I see it says "Kadijevic" on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, that will be corrected. You said one man was killed on the Serbian side in that conflict. Were there any victims on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think Josip Jovic has frequently been mentioned as the first victim of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To what extent were the Plitvice lakes as the site of the conflict distant from Plaski and Saborsko, and how did this influence the situation in Saborsko, because you made this link, so how did the conflict in Plitvice affect the situation in Plaski?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, while this was going on in Plitvice, in Plaski some four or 5.000 people gathered. Not only from Plaski, there were Serbs from Kordun and Gorski Kotar who had come for the church celebration. And then news began to arrive from Plitvice about the conflict. We had our own internal security apart from the police. Those four from Saborsko didn't turn up for work that day, so we had our own security, and we heard that a Golf was approaching which refused to stop, and that it was on its way to the police station in Plaski. I arrived in the police station. Dusan Latas was there; he was the commander of that office, branch office, and there were four men inside. Three of them introduced themselves as employees of the state security from Karlovac. Another, the fourth one had a semi-automatic rifle. He was wearing civilian clothes, but he was carrying a camouflage uniform and a cap with a chequer-board emblem in a plastic bag. He arrived late. He was part of that special purpose unit and he was late. So they were taking him to Saborsko. And then our internal security men arrived, and I was there, and for their own security we disarmed that group. And because the crowd was threatening and there was a possibility of incidents, because rumours were arriving of hundreds of dead at Plitvice. You know how these rumours spread. We detained them for a day and then we let them go on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that everything was as had been agreed until the 31st of March, 1991, and then the situation change. Did anything else change apart from the arrest of these four?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The branch office of the police station from Plaski did not cover Saborsko, in operative terms. A strong unit appeared there under the command of Josip Turkovic. They numbered some 60 men, and they established a police station or a point or whatever you want to call it in Saborsko. And this was not what had been agreed upon. They cut us off from Korenica, and that's how it was until November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said on the eve of the event in Plitvice on the 30th of March a bus passed through Saborsko and Turkovic was inside. Did you say that? Is he the man who established the police station in Saborsko or was it someone else?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to clarify this. In Ogulin there was a police station. And within that police station there was some kind of platoon or squad, some 50 or 60 men who are called the special purpose MUP unit. And their commander was Josip Turkovic. They passed through Plaski because on your way from Ogulin to Saborsko you have to pass through Plaski, if you take that road. They passed through between 2.00 and 3.00 a.m., so they did it in secret and they cut off the road on that day. After the 31st, no one could pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a question in connection with what you said. You said that they set up some kind of police station or unit in Saborsko and they wouldn't let anyone pass through. What do you mean by "anyone"? And what did it mean for Plaski and for you personally?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for Plaski, it meant being completely cut off. As we had voted at our referendum and made a political decision that our local commune was part of Korenica municipality, we relied on them for all issues that we previously had to go to Ogulin for. We started getting supplies from there, foodstuffs, staples. In Plaski we didn't even have a bakery to make bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When one looks at the map, to the west of Plaski is Ogulin. Is that correct? To the north-west? Or maybe even to the north.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: More to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And Saborsko is on the other side of the road. So was there any other way leading from Plaski to Korenica, apart from the one running through Saborsko? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was an uncertain road. It went through the forest, from Licka Jesenica via Javornik towards Rudopolje and then on to Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And was that road or track in normal use?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was used only by the forestry management people. It was unsafe. It was in poor condition. It was just a forest track.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Up to the time when the police station in Saborsko was established, was road did you take to go to Korenica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: From Plaski when you go to Korenica, you pass through Plavca Draga Licka Jesenica, Saborsko, Poljanak, Plitvice, and then you reach Korenica. It's an asphalt road. In certain parts it's very narrow, but still it can be used by trucks and cars for normal transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened after the 31st of March in respect of this road and you were travelling along that road? Was it possible to pass through or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: When the situation at Plitvice calmed down, after the JNA had arrived and established that buffer zone, that police station in Saborsko remained, at the entrance towards Kuselj they had a check-point, and they searched and maltreated anyone who wanted to pass through. So for many people from Plaski it was impossible to travel along that road. I couldn't because I would have been arrested, as would have all those participating in local government or the police in Plaski. Anyone who was a public figure could not travel through Saborsko. They let through only those people they needed because we had the same electricity supply lines, same telephone lines. They would let them through, to make repairs. Nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in Plaski, where there was several thousand people, there was no bakery. So how did you solve the problem of supplies?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these were enormous problems. People had to bake bread at home. Women baked the bread on their own, and we brought in flour through that forest road. And there were lots of problems. Trucks would get stuck in the mud, they would topple over. It was a very difficult situation. We had a little health station which we had transformed into a health centre, and the doctors were very -- permitted very enthusiastic, but it was very difficult to transport people to hospital if they needed to be transported there urgently; for example, for an appendix operation. It would take about three hours to get them to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would it have been faster if it had been possible to pass through Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you try to solve this situation by talking to your neighbours from Saborsko? Did you have any political talks or negotiations? That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, on our side. On our side we authorised Mihajlo Knezevic. At that time he was either the secretary of the Licka Jesenica local commune, which is the closest one to Saborsko, or maybe he was even employed in the administration. But anyway, he was a very respectable, prominent person locally. Everybody knew him. And he was authorised to negotiate. We asked simply that the road be open and that the -- those armed men be removed, and we offered the children of Saborsko to come to school in Plaski, because Plaski had a very nice school with central heating, and we said that teachers from Plaski could go and work over there, so we tried to settle things to have all the local services functioning properly until agreement could be reached. However, whenever we were on the point of reaching an agreement, the Croatian authorities would do something to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of what happened on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the summer, first the check-point was set up. Then that first Josip Turkovic group went back by another route through Slunj, Primislje, and Trzic. They went back to Ogulin. And the unit arrived from Duga Resa. That's a large village near Karlovac in Croatia. And they continued holding that check-point and preventing normal communication between Plaski and Korenica, because the local population in Saborsko, at least that was my feeling, was willing to reach an agreement with Plaski. But later on, on two occasions, they called these reinforcements; I don't think they were reinforcements, I think it was pouring oil on the flames, some 200 armed men arrived from Zagreb, commanded by Luka Hodak, bringing weapons and arming the entire population of Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You described the situation. So please tell us now, were there any armed conflicts at that time in that area?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the same day, when there was a conflict at Plitvice, there was also an incident in Vojinovac. That's at the edge of the Serb majority territory when you come from the direction of Ogulin. And unfortunately a Serb who was not a member of the MUP killed another Serb who was in one of the local village patrols at a railway barrier. This was an enormous problem, and we were deeply concerned about it. After that, a special purpose unit of the MUP of the Krajina in Plaski was established. After we had separated from Ogulin and after the check-point in Saborsko had been set up, there were only eight policemen left in Plaski. These were the only eight armed people. And on the other side they were already establishing the ZNG, the National Guard Corps, Croatia was jingling its weapons. There were threats in Pakrac, in Dvor Na Uni. We saw terrible images on television. And I went to Knin and asked Mr. Martic to help and to arm the reserve force so that we could enlarge that police station in Plaski to increase our security and respond to any possible incursions by Croatian forces from the direction of Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you go to see Mr. Martic in Knin to ask him to reinforce the police force in Plaski?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was in May of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was your position at the time? Did you hold an office in Plaski at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the president of the conference of local communes. Being the president of the largest local commune, I became president of the conference of local communes. We called it either the conference or the association of local communes, but it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When in May of 1991 you went to see Mr. Martic, I suppose you went to Knin. Can you tell us: What did you agree on with him, if anything?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I explained the situation to him as it was. I asked him to help us with weapons. I told him that we had some people who had gone through police training in the army. You know, at the time we had people who had served in the regular JNA within the military police units, and upon completing their military service they became reserve members of police force, military police. So I asked for additional manpower to expand that force. We were afraid of the Plaski MUP; that was our greatest fear. Mr. Martic then said that the weapons could be given only to the people who had gone through the training, who had some authorities, because he didn't want some kind of a cowboy police suddenly to emerge in Plaski. And then I asked him what was the procedure. And he told me that people who wished to do so could go to Golubic, to Knin, where they would attend a brief period of training and they would be issued with long-barrelled weapons there and that following that they would become members of the special purpose unit in Plaski. He told me personally that it wouldn't hurt me if I went through a similar training because I was overweight at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, did you accept this suggestion and what happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I took a group of 25 men. In late May, in early June, we went to Golubic to the camp site for training.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I may. Your Honour, I'm not going to -- I'm not exactly objecting to this evidence, but I do have an inquiry, which is why none of this information was contained on the 65 ter summary. And in fact it surprised us so much that it wasn't because of course we know all about this and I have questions I'm going to ask the witness about these matters, because we have information about this. But we inquired of the Defence specifically if there was additional information to add to the 65 ter summary. They provided a few extra pieces but nothing about any of this. And I'm just -- I just wonder why -- this is obviously relevant and pertinent information. This is directly about the accused. I just wonder why this wasn't contained on the Rule 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, if you are not exactly objecting, is this an appropriate time to ask the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, perhaps not, but I'm happy to raise it at another time. But I'm really what I'm thinking, I'm thinking ahead. I'm thinking first of all about the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're thinking aloud?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm not thinking aloud. I'm thinking ahead about future witnesses, and I wanted to make the point now, when it's fresh, when the situation has arisen, we have other witnesses where we anticipate this situation arising. We have pressed this matter again and again and again and again about the 65 ter summaries, and it never gets resolved. And so I -- perhaps it wasn't the right time to raise it and for that I apologise, but I raise it with respect to future witnesses. And also, I think that perhaps there could be an answer about why it wasn't provided for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want an answer now or can we get the answer just at the end of the witness's testimony in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm in your hands, Your Honour, on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we keep it until then?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had gone for training in late May with 25 men. What kind of a training was it? How long did it last and what happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I skipped over an important detail. Prior to all of these contacts I had with Mr. Martic, members of police branch office signed an obligation to transfer to the Krajina MUP, they pledged loyalty to that, and that was supported by the conference of local communes. At the time Mr. Martic was man number one within the Krajina police. Naturally I addressed him asking for assistance that was quite legal. Now to go back to my earlier story. We went via that forest road there. We were wearing civilian clothes and we were unarmed. We went to Knin. We came to Golubic, to the camp site there. We received camouflage uniforms there. I remember that in our pockets we found messages written in a female hand, such as "may God protect you, brother" and similar type messages. These were just ordinary uniforms made out of a plain type of material. We started with our training. And it was a bit unusual for me, because they taught us how to load and unload a weapon, and for me, who had served in the army, that was quite an easy task, but there were some people there who had never been in the army. At the camp itself there was a wooden type of wall, and we practiced climbing it with a rope, and on that wall there was a slogan saying: This is where terrorism ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How long did this training last for?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: 21 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What were you taught there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: We spent the longest time on establishment, movement, sweeping of terrain. Simple military training. Getting to know your weapons. How to handle them and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So after 21 days of training, what happened then? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: We went back to Plaski in a bus. We travelled to a place called Javornik -- or, rather, to Rudopolje, and then from there we walked to the train station in Javornik. There were still some train service, and I think we took train to Plaski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have uniforms, weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had uniforms, weapons, and we established at the secondary school in Plaski, which was shut down at the time, a headquarters of sorts. The 25 of us lived there, slept there for several months, because the police station wasn't functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well where did you get your weapons and uniforms, because you said that you had gone to Golubic without them. How did you obtain this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: At the camp site in Golubic, there was several makeshift houses, because this used to be some kind of a youth camp before these events, and there was some kind of a warehouse there. I didn't know those people, but you know how it is. Under similar circumstances, they just give you these things. You take them over. I had no time to really meet these people, to get to know them and their names. We were issued with combat sets on our way home. Each of us received some 150 bullets or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, think it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed. We will take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry the Chamber will take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, at the break I was kindly requested by the interpreters to pause after putting my question to you and hearing your answer, and the same request was put to you. So we have to bear that in mind. You said that after the 21 days of training you returned to Plaski with the people you attended training and that you were put up at school there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the total head count of the police force was at the time you returned from training.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: There were eight members from before, and there were 25 of us. Another group of 16 or 18 people went to Golubic, but they returned a bit sooner than we did. Counting all the members of the active and reserve forces, there were about 50 people in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What were the people who underwent the training, including yourself and the members of the active police force, tasked with? What sort of difficulties did you face?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: We faced the same kind of difficulties as were faced by others elsewhere. We had many criminals who seized every opportunity they had for private gain. We had several instances of robbery, burglaries, even murders. We tried to combat crime. We arrested people. In addition to that, we also carried out traffic control. I personally took part in mopping up the area, which was part of our training. All in all, we were trying to secure the area, both from within and from without. But I have to tell you that I was not involved in the classic type of policing, as was Mr. Latas because Mr. Latas had several police professionals, including forensic officers there. Therefore, I was not involved in that sort of work at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Dusan Latas. What position did he hold at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the police substation, which later on became the public security station. He was its chief. Dusan Latas had secondary education and specialised in administrative law matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: His last name is Latas. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that you helped in securing the area of Plaski. Who were you securing the area against at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, Croatia already had the National Guard Corps, which had as its members HDZ members, who were known to attack Serbian institutions, specifically in the area of Ogulin. On several occasions coffee shops frequented by Serbs were blown up. One such shop was owned by Rade Milanovic. This was at the entrance to Ogulin. It was blown up on several occasions until it was fully destroyed. These were mostly coffee shops and restaurant establishments. There was another such instance --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is enough. This took place in Ogulin, which is near to Plaski. But you in Plaski, who did you protect yourself from?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: We chose to live in the SAO Krajina and we opted for the Krajina police to do the policing. Our duty was to materialise the will of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any military installation of the JNA in Plaski?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: When speaking of Plaski, again I have to refer to the entire area from Vojinovac to Licka Jesenica, and we referred to it as the Plaski valley. In the centre of Plaski, there was a barracks with the medical supplies depot and a warehouse which was owned by the federal direction for commodities which were secured by JNA unit in Plaski. This unit was less than 20 men strong. It was led by Sergeant Ivica Gace, who was a Croat by ethnicity. Some 10 to 12 kilometres away from Plaski, there was barracks in Licka Jesenica on the railway track leading from Plaski to Knin. There was a depot of fuel there, the capacity was 7.000 tonnes, and it was secured by a platoon of 30 soldiers. The commander of the barracks was called Bruno Pecirep, Captain First Class, Croat by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough. Did there come a time when armed conflicts arose in Plaski in the course of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: A serious armed conflict took place on the 22nd of June, when the Croatian forces set out from the direction of Josipdol toward Plaski. In the area of Vojnovci, just outside Vojnovci, an armed conflict occurred. We foiled this attempt at a breakthrough, and it was then that a full communications blockade was imposed in the Ogulin area. Dane Bunjevac, who was the commander of the first platoon was killed, and Bogdan Letica was wounded, and I'm speaking on the Serb side. On the Croatian side there were also some casualties that they reported on over the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Croatian forces set out from the direction of Josipdol and that you managed to prevent the attack. Who were you referring to when you said "we," and how was it that you managed to crush the attack?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time in addition to the unit I commanded over and in addition to the police unit, the regular police force commanded by Dusan Latas, we had already set up a detachment of the Territorial Defence, so it had been in existence since July of 1991. I know that in the logistics base in Karlovac, I believe it was Skondric there, who -- they had signed up for 650 semi-automatic rifles, the detachment had already been set up, the TO staff was established, and it was commanded over by the Captain First Class Nikola Dokmanovic, who was part of the reserve force. They were already carrying out their duties as the TO within the armed forces of Yugoslavia. The fighting broke out between my unit and the Croatian MUP units and paramilitary units. I know there were paramilitary units as well because I could see them. Some of them were in civilian clothes. And this was in the area of Sabljacke Drage, between Josipdol and Plaski. Infantry fire was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any positions in the area, any check-points or any sort of organised positions?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I spoke in haste. We had a check-point along the boundary, the ethnic boundary, because Vojinovac was the settlement on the very edge along the ethnic lines. It was a Serb village. And we carried out patrols from the village of Vajin Vrh, all the way down to Vojinovac. And that's the area halfway between Josipdol and Plaski. We controlled the road own our side, and they had already established their check-point and controlled their side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How did the conflict come about?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the course of the night --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please pause before answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please pause.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The night before the 22nd, there were squirmishes. Infantry fire could be heard, because their MUP unit, which was manning the check-point, did not allow anyone to pass into Plaski, not even a funeral equipment. And I remember that, because we didn't have any in Plaski. So it was thus that first gunfire could be heard and then a full-fledged attack broke out, which took part during the night and then continued on for the entire 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will not dwell on this topic, but just tell us, what do you mean by a serious, a fierce attack? What weapons were involved, and how far or how much of the terrain was involved?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: We found out at a later date that on their side all the available MUP forces were involved in the attack, namely 200 to 300 men, whereas we, on our part, engaged the forces we had. I have to say that the Territorial Defence occupied the positions that we managed to keep until 1995, and I'm speaking about the 22nd of July. The attack on their part involved infantry and artillery weapons alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You're talking about the 22nd of July, 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like in Plaski in the aftermath of these clashes?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: After the 22nd of July, Plaski was fully surrounded. The scarce supplies that were trickling in by that time were completely discontinued. We were surrounded on all sides, on the one hand we had Slunj, then the military grounds there, all the way to Ogulin. And then from Ogulin, beside the mount Mala Kapevla [phoen], you had the Croatian population there, Stajnica, Lipice, Saborsko, and all the way down to the Plitvice lakes. We were completely surrounded and had to set up circular defence. We had to deploy to the lines whatever weapons and manpower we had in all the directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that Plaski was fully isolated, can you tell us what of the food and medical supplies, what of the electricity supplies, how did you tackle these problems?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: From that date on, we no longer had electricity. We tried to manage the best we could with the medications we had. We tried to pull out the wounded, through -- along a forest road. It's a bit difficult to explain it here, but the area is a vast woodland area of very dense pine wood, very tall, some 800 to 900 metres. The area was not easily trafficable. Besides, we had problems with the power supplies. We had no telephone lines. The children who were attending schools outside the Plaski area found it hard to return back. The post office was unable to function and the people who were retired could not receive their pension. There were around 7.000 of us, and we were fully surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When it came to Plaski and under those circumstances, can you tell us what sort of position the JNA found itself in, and I mean the JNA garrisons in the area.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: The fate that befell the Serbs in the area also befell the JNA. Croatia at the time had declared the JNA an aggressor and did not allow them to move about. We have to note that the first barracks that fell into the hands of the Croats was the one in Ogulin. The JNA units were also under a full blockade, but they were able to communicate with the Slunj training grounds where the relocated command of the 5th Army was. They were also blocked, but it was possible for them to leave the Plaski barracks and to reach the Slunj training grounds. However, along the way there were also places under Croatian control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any military actions undertaken by the Croats against the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that the first barracks that fell into the hands of the Croats was the one in Ogulin, which took place in September of 1991. In addition to the Ogulin barracks, in the vicinity of both Ogulin and Josipdol, there were several barracks at Ostarije and Skradnik. At Skradnik there was a weapons depot. I know for a fact that more than 100 pieces of infantry weapons were stored there. Over 700 mortars were stored there. And large numbers of guns of smaller calibres, namely ZIS, the field gun. I know this because Lieutenant-Colonel Radakovic - I don't know what his position was at the time - he mobilised, he recruited a group of persons into the JNA to secure the facility at Skradnik, because the manpower present at the time in those facilities was leaving the area, not only Serbs, and they wanted to prevent these facilities from falling into the hands of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I were to say that this depot in Skradnik was a large JNA depot, would I be correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that in Licka Jesenica there was a large storage containing fuel, about 7.000 tonnes, was that the JNA warehouse?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any warehouses there in addition to these two?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Ostarije 1 and 2. Ostarije is a settlement near Ogulin and Josipdol and there was an ammunition warehouse there, a depot containing artillery and rocket ordinance. It was blown up. It didn't fall into anyone's hands. It was blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why the JNA blew it up?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA blew it up because it was impossible for them to evacuate the supplies. They were able to evacuate the people. And as for supplies, the ammunition, it was blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to make our break. Or, rather, we have to pause. You described the situation in Plaski as one of complete isolation. Did you try to resolve the situation by talking to the people from Saborsko, to your neighbours from Saborsko, even under those circumstances? Did you attempt this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was precisely the most active negotiations time. We even asked the JNA, which at the time was still a multi-ethnic force, to mediate and to give certain guarantees that the people living there would be completely safe, that nobody would be sent away from Plaski. We simply asked them to liberate that road. However, as I told you, when we came close to some kind of a settlement - and this was in September - the reinforcement came to Saborsko from Zagreb. They passed through Lipice, Stajnica and en route they captured our guards, members of the TO. They also captured two active policemen on their way back from Korenica. And they captured civilians who were minors, the children of a man who lived in a forest. It sounds strange, but there was this man living alone with his six children in the forest, 10 kilometres away from any civilisation. So these children came and told us that they had been released but other people had been captured and taken to Saborsko by these people. This ruined all of our plans to achieve a peaceful settlement via negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But we know nothing about these negotiations. Who negotiated with whom from Saborsko? Do you remember any of those facts, and please describe, very briefly, if you do. What kind of a settlement were you close to reaching when this armed group came from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already mentioned, on our side the negotiations team was led by Mihajlo Knezevic, as he used to be a teacher in Saborsko before the war and he was a prominent citizen, a well known person in that area. He led the delegation. I don't remember the exact names of people participating on their side. I think that this man had some problems with breathing. He had some machine that helped him breathe, so he was a man from Saborsko who was participating on their side. His name might have been Mataj, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What were your requests and what did they accept, and what was in fact ruined when this group arrived?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: We requested that the road be freed from Licka Jesenica to the Plitvice lakes, that it be freed for civilian transportation and for supplies. We asked that the people who were there withdraw, that they surrender weapons to the JNA. In addition to the four policemen who used to be policemen in Plaski -- we wanted, rather, those four to remain there, and all other armed forces we wanted them to surrender their weapons to the Plaski police and to the Territorial Defence, and we wanted the JNA to guarantee that the road would be freed. And so that the JNA itself could use it, and so that the civilians from Plaski could use it too. We had no electricity. We had no water. We needed generators. We needed fuel. We were unable to procure any of those supplies, as long as that road was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time in Plaski, Saborsko and surrounding areas, when an armed conflict broke out and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Even before the month of September, that is to say in August, since Saborsko is higher above the sea level than Licka Jesenica, there was a dominant feature, a hill called Borik that was under their control, which enabled them to see Licka Jesenica as though it lay on their palm. So they kept firing and thus preventing people from working the land. So back in August I transferred a platoon to the school in Licka Jesenica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're talking about August. August of which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may continue, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you said you deployed a platoon. With what mission?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: The platoon was tasked with securing, providing safety to the people working in the fields. The winter comes early there, so people have to finish all of the field work in a timely manner, before the winter comes, and that's exactly what they were doing. They only responded to the fire if they were attacked. And as soon as they responded seriously, all provocations ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that an armed group of people came from Zagreb. Do you know how many people were in that group who were armed? And what kind of weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: We established that following the exchange. But I have to tell you the entire event. I apologise, but it will take some time. I told you that this group arrived from Zagreb under command of Luka Hodak. They travelled on the road from Stajnica, Lipice, and then to Kriz via a forest road to Saborsko. Since there were over 200 of them, they of course were more powerful, and they captured four of our men, securing that road. They captured these four from Licka Jesenica, then they captured two policemen on their way back. I happened to pass by. I was on my way to Licka Korenica, the late Major Latas was with me, and they captured him and I managed to escape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, can I interrupt you. I think you're taking rather too long. The question to you was: You mentioned that an armed group of people came from Zagreb. Do you know how many people were in that group who were armed and what kind of weapons did they have? You have just told us, after a very long story, that there were over 200. You still haven't told us the weapons they had. Try to listen to the questions, Witness, and try to answer as directly as you possibly can to the questions. That they came via the forest will be established. If counsel wants to know that, he will ask you that. Don't -- listen to the question and answer the question. Mr. Milovancevic, please try to control the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I put a question to you which you heard, and you said you would give an extensive explanation. You have given us the context on the basis of which we can understand how you got this information. So some people were imprisoned and then exchanged?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologised to His Honour. Precisely so. What I wanted to say was that I had first-hand information, because Vlado Vukovic was taken prisoner and fell into our hands. He was then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're still not answering the question, sir. Mr. Milovancevic, you are still not pursuing the question that you had asked. The question that you asked was: How many were these people, what kind of weapons did they have. We have been told there were over 200. We don't know what weapons they had. We are now being told other stories and you are allowing this to go on. Try to bring the witness to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
