utterances.text: Witness, we must be very precise. I will put a question to you. Please answer it directly, and, if need be, I will put additional questions. This is what is proposed by Their Honours, and this is the usual procedure in these proceedings. Please tell us what these people had, what kind of weapons they had. If anything else needs to be established, I will ask you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: There were about 12 trucks, 200 people, and they brought infantry weapons for all the remaining population in Saborsko. They all arrived bearing weapons. They brought at least 82-millimetre mortars, an anti-aircraft gun of 20 millimetres, at least one, one Browning. A 12.7-millimetre machine-gun, and a recoilless gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said all of this happened in September 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the arrival of this group ruined your negotiation with the inhabitants of Saborsko about a peaceful settlement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened in Saborsko after the arrival of this group? How did the situation develop further? I'm referring to the group that arrived in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a shooting into the air. People were celebrating. The people who were imprisoned were beaten. They had to pass through the gauntlet and they were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the relative strength of these forces in Saborsko as compared to those in Plaski and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Saborsko then became a stronghold with about 400 men under arms. They had all the weapons I have listed, artillery weapons. They deployed themselves along the road and all the points leading towards Licka Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they deployed themselves along the road and that all the points, what points are you referring to? Do these points have names or labels of any kind?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the dominant elevations, Borik and Sivnik in this case. Those are the two dominant elevations between Saborsko and Licka Jesenica. They took these elevations and fortified them. And in depth, and I know this first-hand, too, because I carried out reconnaissance, Saborsko is a long village. From Saborsko to Kuselj, there's about six kilometres. Along the road they made dugouts and dug trenches covered with logs, which means that they were preparing seriously for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any conflicts between the JNA and the forces in Saborsko before November 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: JNA facilities were targeted when they targeted Plaski. And this was -- this happened for the first time in September 1991. Whereas a serious attack occurred in November when there was an attack launched on the barracks in Licka Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the conflict arose because the forces in Saborsko were targeting Licka Jesenica and Plaski? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: They were not able to hit Plaski from Saborsko, because the distance between Saborsko and Plaski exceeds the range of the weapons they had. But they did shoot a test from Kapela and Modrasa [phoen] from the direction of Josipdol and Ogulin. From Saborsko, you can see exceptionally well, because it's higher up than Licka Jesenica in terms of height of elevation, and the people shooting at us were not able to see. So they were guided by the people from Saborsko. They were able to hit without missing their targets. They hit the clinic in Licka Jesenica which was clearly designated with the Red Cross, and a nurse was killed of that occasion; her name was Javorka Vukelic. And another one, Dusanka Grba, was seriously injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, you are an inhabitant of Plaski. You reside there. And you are talking about an attack on the barracks in Licka Jesenica and the transference of fire. You say that they were guiding the fire from Saborsko. How do you know this, where did you get this information?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time I was there on the spot. Around the 4th of November, or in early November, this very sensitive point -- called Glibodolski Kriz -- it's a crossing. When you come from Licka Jesenica you reach this crossing and we had a guard there. This was attacked. Two men were injured and they withdrew. So I led a group, which had to take that crossing again. We came -- fell into the fire targeting Licka Jesenica and came into conflict with the forces which were on the way, on their way to undertake an infantry assault or take the barracks. I was in command of the group that was on its way to retake Glibodolski Kriz, the crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say this was on the 24th of November, 1991 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 4th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: -- and that their forces were attacking the JNA barracks in Licka Jesenica. Which forces were these?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: These were the forces of the Croatian MUP and ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion was the barracks in Licka Jesenica taken?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: The fighting went on for several days and the attack was beaten back, thanks to assistance from Plaski. A soldier was killed. I think his name was Zeljko Gajsak or some such Croatian last name. He was an ethnic Croat. He was an active-duty soldier and he was killed. A few others were killed too. On the Croatian side, another soldier was killed, whom I saw personally. He was wearing a camouflage uniform. He was killed by some sort of large calibre weapon. We couldn't identify him. He was buried next to the Licka Jesenica railway line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you participated in that conflict on the 4th of November, 1991, near the barracks in Licka Jesenica. How did you establish that the fire on the barracks, the artillery fire on the barracks was guided by the Croatian forces in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: The forces in Saborsko, not only guided the fire but also attacked the barracks on the other side of the railway line. They arrived and the attack was repulsed. When withdrawing toward Saborsko, they passed by Vukelic Poljana, it's a little hamlet in Licka Jesenica and Branko Vukalic, Sapina, was killed on the threshold of his own house. And they boasted about this. They said, well, they haven't managed to take the barracks, but at least they had killed a Chetnik. This so-called Chetnik was about 50 years old and was on his way to see to his cattle in the barn. So he wasn't engaged in any military activity. He was on his own threshold. And I heard about this from imprisoned Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether in November 1991 the JNA took any action to defend its facilities and lift the blockade of the roads in the area?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA was in a difficult situation. In the area it was completely blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just going to object to the leading nature of that last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the objection is that you are asking a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have that impression, but to avoid any problems, I will reformulate the question, I will rephrase it. I think that would be the best thing to do, because I don't wish to put leading questions. If you agree?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I agree, but I also warn you that the answer to the question is already known to the witness based on the leading question that you asked. Carry on. Rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the mention of Mr. Cedomir Bulat, a JNA colonel, mean anything to you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How did you meet him? How did you get to know him? On what occasion?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the first time I met him was when the former commander of that barracks, Bruno Pecirep and Ivica Gace, the commander of the barracks in Plaski, who were both Croats, were taken by me to the military training ground because their safety was under threat because of some public statements they had made, and I took them to the army command and handed them over to Colonel Cedo Bulat for their own safety. That's when I got to know him. He was a colonel. I think he was the chief of the operations department, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And where was he then?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: He was at the military training grounds in Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does Tactical Group 2 of the JNA mean something to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I know that Cedo Bulat was in command of TG 2, and I know that it was the oldest command on the ground, so to say, and we were all subordinate to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that tactical group appeared. You said you were all subordinate to it, so where did it appear?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: This was when serious cooperation began between the Territorial Defence in Plaski and the JNA units to defend the barracks in Licka Jesenica. That was in early November 1991. I'm sure it was then, and maybe before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see on the monitor a document from the 65 ter list of the OTP, and it's marked 1246.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before it turns up on the monitor, can you tell us: Tactical Group 2, what army did it belong to? What army was it part of?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army, the 5th Army District or the so-called 5th Army, the Zagreb army as it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have before you on the monitor a document now. Please take a look at it. Could we look at the upper left-hand corner. Thank you. Can you read out to us what it says in the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: "Command of the 5th Military District, strictly confidential, number, 23rd October 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Underneath that there is a brief heading. Can you tell us what it says?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: "The formation of TG 2 order."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, you read that as formation of TG 2. Can you tell us what this means to you in whole words, the expansion.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Tactical Group 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Underneath this text, towards the bottom of the page, could we look at points two and three of this order. Could you please read out the text of these two points.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: "The command of TG 2 is to be formed, comprising senior officers from the composition of the command and the units of the 5th Military District according to the appended list. Colonel Cedomir Bulat is hereby appointed commander of TG 1. He's the head of the department for operative affairs." I apologise to the interpreters. Item 3: "The task of the command of Tactical Group 2 is to unite or unify the operations of the units of the JNA at the training ground in Slunj and the units of TO Veljun and Plaski in the area of responsibility. Slunj, Veljun, Plaski, in the area of responsibility Slunj, Veljun, Perjasica, Primislje, Plaski, Grabovac, Koranski Leskovac, Cetingrad, Tactical Group 2..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's quite enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see page 2 of this document, and there are a total of two pages in this document so that we can see who signed it. In B/C/S it is 7806. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read the seal and the signature?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Command of the military district." I don't see the number of the military district. And then -- that's what it says on this stamp. Then it says: General -- "Colonel General Zivota Avaramovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that all of you were subordinated to the Tactical Group 2. You meant the TG 2 of the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Already at that time the unit which was under my command was within the brigade of TO of Plaski, that is to say, that unit was disbanded. It no longer existed as the special purpose unit. Rather, members of that unit were transferred to the active police force and then the rest of them became members of the TO based on their place of residence. I told you that our unit was established on the 1st of July, and in early September it became a brigade with 3 Battalion. It was a brigade of the Territorial Defence of Plaski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was the attitude of the JNA towards that, Plaski TO unit and other TO units?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that according to the then valid legislation, the TO forces were armed forces, but the JNA had the direct command, that is to say, the most senior commanders also had the TO under their command as well as police. That was a well known principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender this document into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted as an Defence exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 960.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Your Honours, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may take the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, sir, we saw the order to establish Tactical Group 2, it came from the 5th Military District of the JNA. Do you know whether this order was implemented, was carried out, and which forces comprised TG 2, in case it was implemented?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that it was implemented. I know that Colonel Bulat became commander of the tactical group, and I know that our brigade became part of it and that we were directly subordinated to Colonel Bulat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said: "Our brigade became part of it and was directly subordinated." Which was your brigade, just so that we avoid any confusion?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: The brigade of the Plaski Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Tactical Group 2 carried out any operations in that area, in November, in late 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that an order came to lift the siege of Plaski, of our entire municipality, and military facilities by breaking down Ustasha stronghold in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who conveyed the order to you? Can you explain to us what you mean by saying the Ustasha stronghold in Saborsko? Why don't you address that first, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's how I have to call that stronghold because just before the order was issued a terrible incident took place at Gribodolski Kriz, or crossing, where three men were savagely killed, people from Plaski. And this was part of the operation attacking the Licka Jesenica barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Witness. You were asked a question: Do you know whether Tactical Group 2 carried out any operations in that area, in November, in late 1991. You told us how an order came. Can you tell us just by yes or no, did Tactical Group 2 carry out any operations in that area in November 1991? I want one word from you, either yes, or no, or I don't know." It's the only time I will allow two words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen to the questions and try to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that, yes, operations were carried out, and then you explained that the purpose of those operations was to destroy the Ustasha forces in Saborsko; I'm paraphrasing your words. And my question was: Why are you using that term, "Ustasha forces"? Just briefly. You mentioned this crossing, Glibodolski Kriz?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the first time I used that term. I think that it was a watershed in the line of thinking of all of us in Plaski, because we were able to see just what kind of forces those were after that massacre which took place at Glibodolski Kriz, or crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that because of this massacre which took place at Glibodolski Kriz, you referred to these forces in Saborsko as Ustasha forces?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: So far I have spoken of Croatian forces of ZNG and Croatian MUP forces. However, after seeing with my own eyes how ZNG and MUP operated in the field, I can tell you that the term "Ustasha" is too mild for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please briefly describe what happened at Glibodolski Kriz which prompted you to use this language?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: When this road was liberated, the road leading to Glibodolski Kriz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: From which point, please? Or rather, when?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 7th or 8th of November, within that attack on the barracks in Licka Jesenica. That attack took three days. When that crossing was taken once again, we saw a fresh mold of earth that was created with a loader. Since we didn't have any equipment with us, we just took the soil away with our hands, and we saw that there were two corpses and a horse carcass. And then next to it, we saw the remains of a Fico car, which is the smallest automobile produced in the former Yugoslavia. And next to it we found a human ear cut off, which indicated that most likely people who had been in that car were killed. Next to Fico was a tractor with a small trailer, also destroyed. In that mold of soil, under the carcasses of horses, we excavated the corpses of three people, and their names were Susnjar Milan, Bogdan --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreters didn't hear the third name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned three men. What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: All of them were Serbs. Petrovic Bogdan used to be a member of the unit which I commanded. That day he had civilian trousers on and a shirt with the Krajina police symbol on it. The other two were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the state of these people when you found them? You said that they were dead, and you found them under carcasses of horses.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: The ear that we found in the car belonged to Petrovic Bogdan. On his leg he had a leather belt tied, leather belt used for horses, and it was that belt that they used to hang him from a tree. He had over 40 stabs, knife stabs, mostly in the area of genitals, which means that he was castrated alive practically. This is what the doctor told me. He obviously knew why he made that conclusion. That was the corpse of Bogdan Petrovic. The next one was Susnjar Milan, nicknamed Mijak. He had a large ring. I knew the man personally. He had a large signet ring, and it was cut off and his hand was cut off. And he had been mistreated while alive too. And the last person, the last Susnjar, apparently died due to mortar fire, near the tractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said, sir, that you found the corpses of these people under the carcasses of horses. How did you establish the cause of their death?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: We pushed aside the soil. There were about 30 of us. Mostly members of police. Dusan Latas was there. We removed the soil with our hands and then we pulled away the horses, their carcasses, and then we transported human corpses to a place called Janja, which is the area where they were from. We put them in wooden crates, and we called in a surgeon. We cut off their clothes to see what kind of injuries they had. I made three Polaroid photographs as we were doing that, and they exist in the centre for investigation of war crimes. I hope that we will be able to locate them and send them to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milovancevic. Can we make sure that we have the names of these three victims on our transcript. One name has not been understood before, I think. So it was Petrovic Bogdan. And the next one was Milan -- what was the name again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Susnjar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And the third one? Can you give us the name of the third victim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also Susnjar, but the first name is Bogdan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just to conclude that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for us, Mr. Milovancevic. Does it mean we have two Susnjars and we have two Bogdans? The one was Petrovic Bogdan and now there is Bogdan Susnjar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Two first names are identical, Bogdan. There is Bogdan Petrovic and Bogdan Susnjar. And the first name of the other Susnjar is Milan. These are the three victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Before you go on there is also a question that I wish to ask. On what basis was it concluded that the ear that was found belonged to Bogdan, the first Bogdan, Bogdan Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That crossing in that area was under the control of Croatian forces for two days. The car that I described, Fico, was a car produced in Serbia, and it was a car owned by many people there. It belonged to Petrovic and that was the first indication. Next to this seat, as he was sitting somebody through the window cut off his ear, because that's where the ear was found. It was found between the door and the seat, and later on, as we pulled his body out, we saw that an ear was missing on his body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: While we are asking questions about that, may I ask you two things. First, who was the forensic doctor you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can hardly be described as a forensic expert. No, he was a surgeon, Zivko Vrcelj, who used to work as a doctor in our health station. We had no conditions to carry out a proper investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And the other thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the name again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The name again, please, of this surgeon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zivko Vrcelj, V-r-c-e-l-j. Now he works as a doctor in Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And the other thing is, you made an observation before this was the first time you used the word "Ustasha." Do you remember? You said that five minutes ago. What do you mean by this was the first time that you used this word? Not now, but you mean at that time when you -- after you found this scene? Do I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that it was the first time during my testimony here that, when describing that event, I used the word "Ustasha." I said that this event reminded us very strongly about the events of the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said "yes" when I asked you whether Tactical Group 2 was active in that area. When was it? When were they active? And did you have anything to do with their operations?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: After the barracks in Licka Jesenica was defended, I was told by the battalion commander in whose area of responsibility Licka Jesenica, and that was Grba Bogdan, that an order had been issued to lift the siege to deblock the road in order to get to the fuel. I told you that there was 7.000 tonnes of fuel. The JNA needed fuel. They had none, because the other warehouse that they had down the railroad had already been captured by Croats. So this remaining supply was the only supply remaining to the 5th Army. So they issued an urgent order to liberate the road passing through Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see Exhibit 108 on our screens. This is on 65 ter list of OTP, 1248. This is the operations diary of Tactical Group 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the exhibit to come on, could the witness just answer whether, indeed, he did take part in the operations with TG 2. That was part of your question. I don't think it was answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you took part in the Tactical Group 2 action?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I personally commanded over one company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who commanded over the entire action at Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Cedomir Bulat commanded over the entire operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that you had one company under your command. Who made up the company?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the active and reserve police forces, several volunteers from units which were not deployed in that area but rather from Battalions 1 and 2, and some volunteers who were members of the special purpose unit and were then transferred to the TO brigade. There were a total of 60 of us, and it wasn't a proper company, not to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to the document, another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the special purpose unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first part of my evidence, I said that out of the group of people who underwent training in Knin, a special purpose unit was made. These were people from Plaski only, and I commanded over that unit until the 1st of September, 1991. They should not be mixed up or confused with the other special purpose unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you mean that, when you talk of the special purpose unit in this context, you meant the people you were trained were in Knin, in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I should put two more brief questions to the witness before the break, just to finish the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Colonel Bulat was the commander of the Tactical Group 2 and that you commanded over your unit. Did you have an immediate superior officer?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Within these operation, I had the battalion commander, Bogdan Grba, who was my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I'm not mistaken, we normally take the break at 5.15. If I'm correct, then perhaps this would be a convenient time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is, indeed. We shall take the break and come back at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Milovancevic. I had already said so. I may have said it softly, but I thought these microphones are so strong that everybody hears me without me shouting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It was a mistake on my part. I didn't put my headphones on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, we have a document on our screens. I want you to look at the various entries. This is the operations log book of the Tactical Group 2; that's the title of the document. Please, I wish to re-direct your attention to item 3, next to number 3, the column next to that first one, says: Slunj. This is the column at the top of which says: Place, time, and date. And in this particular column, in this particular entry it reads: Slunj, 5 November 1991, 2200 hours. I will read out the entry and you will confirm whether that's correct. It reads as follows: "On the 5th of November, 1991, at around 2200 hours, the following was recorded. Around 1800 hours from the area of Glibodolski Kriz the forces of the ZNG and MUP commenced their operation against SKLG, Licka Jesenica. The combat operations lasted until 2200 hours. The enemy forces were active from the area of Alan and Veliki Sivnik. Artillery returned fire by firing 26 shells." Do you see that text before you, Mr. Medakovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The activities referred to here were leveled against SKLG Licka Jesenica. Can you tell us what this acronym stands for, SKLG?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: It stands for the engine fuel depot. The JNA normally used such acronyms.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the acronym is SKPG.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to say that. It is SKPG, but then it says in translation "sic," so there is an apparent mistake in the original, already. Can we clarify that? Thank you. Please, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, the acronym SKPG, that is the acronym, the way I just read it out now?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the acronym stands for the warehouse of engine fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And therefore in the B/C/S these are the first letters of the three words; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at item 4 of the operations log book. It is located at the very bottom of the page. I am not sure what the page number is in English, but perhaps I should refer you to item 4 and the date, 7 November 1991. I believe, Your Honours, you will be able to locate the entry. It says here: "Against the barracks (SKPG, Licka Jesenica) and upon the forces of the TO Plaski, fire was opened from MB, mortars and Brownings, from -- or by the armed forces of the ZNG from the direction of Saborsko." I believe it says Zuzni Vrh, Bozin Vrh, and other directions.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I would not agree with you in that this reads Zuzni Vrh really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I may have misread it. Let us look at the next entry, which is on page 7798 in the B/C/S. The entry number is 5 and the date again is the 7th of November, 1991. It says Licka Jesenica as the place and the hour is 0250, early in the morning. Next to the date, 7 November, it reads: "Heavy fire from Saborsko and Glibodol is being experienced." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In entry number 6, again it says Licka Jesenica, 7 November 1991, and then several hours, 1630, 1645 and 1700. Then let us read. It says: "A very strong attack on the Licka Jesenica barracks by the ZNG." Below that: Open fire -- "Fire was opened from artillery pieces, 130-millimetre artillery pieces, upon the areas of Mala Kapela Glibodolski Kriz, Vrletna Draga."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I see that, in that it says Vrletna Draga.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the entry number 8, it says 2000 hours, the text reads: "One soldier was killed." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the next entry, entry number 9 it reads: "Slunj, 8 November, 10.45 hours." I apologise to the interpreters for rushing. I am doing my best to take it slowly, but I am speeding. The text reads: "The remains of soldier Zeljko Gajsak were transported by helicopter." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The data here refers to the Licka Jesenica barracks and the attack by the Croatian forces against the barracks. Was this the incident you were referring to as the attack on the barracks that you yourself defended and the attack took place between the 4th and 7th of November?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also stated that a JNA soldier was killed; you even mentioned his name. Is that the soldier whose name is written here?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw his body personally. I believe that I was in the helicopter as he was transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As far as I know, this document from the Prosecution 65 ter list was already admitted into evidence. I will not seek to tender it. I believe we can remove it now from our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with your answers that had to do with the operation around Saborsko involving the Tactical Group 2, I will show you a document marked Exhibit 52 with -- this is the 65 ter document 1251, Exhibit 52. Before we look at the document closely, you told us, Mr. Medakovic, that in Saborsko and the surrounding area there were a lot of men under arms. You called them the Croatian forces under arms. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the top left-hand corner of the document you have before you, the command is stated from where the document originated. Can you read this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: "The command of the 13th K," which probably stands for "corps." "IKM," I know stands for forward command post, "7 November 1991. Hours."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was this document addressed to? Can you infer that from the document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says to the command of Tactical Group 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say below that? What sort of an order is that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: An order for attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 of the document, the following text reads: "The forces of MUP and ZNG Croatia have, for some time now, been fortifying their positions in the areas Borik, Saborsko village, Funtana village, Panjici village and Kuselj. "It is estimated that the strength of the forces in the area stands at around 400 members of paramilitary formations." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 goes on to specify the locations at which these forces were deployed. I will not go into that. I'm interested in page 2 of the document, that's page 2 in the B/C/S, Matsa [phoen] 774, and that's the text that starts after paragraph 3, I don't know the exact page number in the English version, but it is paragraph 4 which starts with the following words: "I have decided." When you find that portion of the text, I would like to put a question to the witness. So the person, the author of the document says: "I have decided as follows: From the present areas, units should be set in motion to reach Licka Jesenica and the village of Kuselj and carry out an attack along the following axes: Kuselj village, Funtana, and Licka Jesenica, Saborsko, with a view to, with support of the air force and artillery simultaneously with a tank attack from the above-mentioned directions, crush and route the enemy formation in the area of Saborsko. Prevent the enemy from pulling out to the north and thus definitely crush the enemy's resistance in the area." Do you see the text, Witness?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In item 5 of the order, there is an order which relates to the 5th Partisan Brigade which should, together with the weapons listed in the order, leave the area where it was currently deployed and move along the axes of Plitvice village, Cerpic, Poljana, Kuselj village, and to attack along the following axes: Kuselj village, Funtana village, with the following mission," and then there is a column there. "To engage in forceful action involving tanks and infantry forces in order to crush the enemy along the said axis, join up with the forces of Tactical Group 2 and in coordinated action with the latter, fully crush the enemy's resistance and prevent them from pulling out to the north." This is the order issued by the command of the 13th Corps to the command of Tactical Group 2. You said that you participated in operations with Tactical Group 2 in order to crush Ustasha forces in Saborsko. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Tactical Group 2 carry out this order?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Tactical Group 2 did it fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now look at another document, which is Exhibit 51. It's a document from the OTP 65 ter list, numbered 1257. The heading on this document is a bit unclear, but we will now look at page 2, items 5 -- no, I apologise. Items 3 and 4 on page 2 of the B/C/S version, which is 9991. Since this is the order containing items 3 and 4, I apologise to the Trial Chamber. I would like them to look for items 3 and 4 in this order. If you are able to follow what I'm telling you, I will show you page 9991, the very top of that page, beginning with two paragraphs. That's all we will be needing from this document. It says here: "The 5th Partisans Brigade" --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. There is a text in English in front of me, which I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Earlier there was a text in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You have it in B/C/S now. It says as follows: "The 5th Partisans Brigade is carrying out combat operations along the axis" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What paragraph are you reading now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is paragraph 2 of item 3 of this order. On page 1, you see paragraph 1, 2 and 3, which are unclear in B/C/S, or illegible, and then the third item has two paragraphs, and I'm reading the second paragraph of item 3, just before item 4 begins. So the second paragraph of item 3 of this order. It should begin with the following words: "The 5th Partisans Brigade."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see it on mine. I'm probably looking at the wrong place. If anybody sees it in the English, I would appreciate any assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to assist, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm advised it is the last sentence on the page starting at item 3. I just didn't see 5th Brigade there, but anyway, I'm told that's the sentence. I see sentence illegible. "... anti-artillery brigade will perform the combat actions in the direction of Kuselj-Funtana-Saborsko in order to develop the forces in the area of..." and then it goes to the next page. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. I found it on page 1 of the English translation. There are two documents on 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So item 3 reads as follows: "The 5th Partisan Brigade is conducting military operations along the axis Kuselj-Funtana-Saborsko, with a mission to crush the forces along the axis of action and in this sector of the village of Saborsko in coordination with the forces of Tactical Group 2, in order to deblock the Licka Jesenica barracks." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Item 4 reads: "I have decided to do the following with the support of air force and coordination of TO forces of Plaski and Licka Jesenica, namely to carry out an attack along the axis Begovic-Licka Jesenica-Saborsko in order to -- or, rather, with the security support from the axis, the village of Glibodol-Korac, with a goal to crush the enemy forces along the axis of operation and to lift the siege of the barracks in the village of Licka Jesenica and then to proceed and in coordination with the forces of the 5th Partisan Brigade to crush the forces in the village of Saborsko." Do you see the text?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The last page of this document, which has a total of sixth pages in B/C/S, marked 7783, is marked "commander." So I would like to look at the last page. Do you see who issued this order, who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Commander Colonel Cedomir Bulat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this colonel a colonel of the JNA in command of Tactical Group 2?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that this document is already an exhibit. It was already admitted into evidence, so I won't move to have it admitted. You and your unit were involved in the JNA operation in order to crush these forces that were mentioned here. Can you tell us briefly whether there was any firing there, whether there was any combat?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I led the attack along the right flank, that is to say, I was on the furthest point on the right. I started out from the village of Momcilovic to Vukelic Poljana, looking from Licka Jesenica I was on the right of the Borik hill, and I went through the canyon in order to link up with these forces from Korenica, the forces of the 5th Partisan Brigade in the sector of Alan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of weaponry did you have, you and you your people. There were a total of 60 people under your command?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: We had infantry weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just find out how do you know there was a total of 60, Mr. Milovancevic? We haven't had this evidence before, or have we?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order not to answer myself, let me put a question to the witness. The witness spoke earlier that he was a commander of one of the units within the battalion under the command of Bogdan Grba. And he mentioned a figure of people under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So we can ask the witness exactly how many people he had under his command.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that pursuant to the order, I was in command of one company, and then I said that it wasn't a fully manned company, because the full strength of a company should be 160 people, whereas I had about 60 men under my command, and I told you which units they had come from. If Your Honour insists, I can repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, you don't have to. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had small arms or infantry weapons. How did combat operations begin? What time of the day and in which manner? Can you describe it briefly?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: It's hard to describe it briefly. There was an attack from the air with two planes. I saw one of them open fire in the sector of Brdina where there was a bunker, and these planes flew over the area, and then this was followed by artillery attack. Light rockets were launched from the sector of Vidakovici village. I think that 130-millimetre guns also provided support. We were unable to see them. They were quite a ways since they have a longer range. I think that a platoon of mortars of 120 millimetres also opened fire, and then all of us went into action following our orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, did you come -- did you find any resistance? Did you meet with any resistance?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: The unit under my command progressed along very unfriendly terrain. It was very a steep slope, and we went through this terrain in order to surprise our enemy. We were not in the middle of our attack yet. We were still walking in a column when we encountered enemy, and we engaged in hand-to-hand combat, and we killed three enemy soldiers. Following that, we took our positions as marksmen and then we started firing -- or, rather, they started firing at us, and then we responded from our positions, and we were in a pine forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that they opened fire on you from their fortified positions. Can you tell us where their fortified positions were, from which they opened fire on you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Looking from their side, that is to say from the side of Saborsko, it was the left flank, going from the Borik Brd -- Borik hill, Brdina and Alan. This was a fortified position that we came across.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that their positions were fortified, can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: This means that there were trenches and that there were trenches with a cover. It wasn't a typical concrete bunker, no. It was an improvised type of bunker that had a cover on top and they opened fire from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to take their positions? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Following that initial contact, following the first close contact and combat with the enemy during which three enemy soldiers died and we had one lightly wounded soldier, wounded by a hand-grenade, we set up a front line, we were able to cover some 600 to 700 metres with our 60 people. So we could already hear the tanks that was the centre of our attack, and the tank produced -- the noise produced by a tank is a very typical one. The period from when the shell is fired until it detonates is a very brief one. Our task was to link up with the forces of the 5th Partisan Brigade, and we were to raise Yugoslav flag once we linked up with them. However, we didn't link up with them, and we came under friendly fire, because from the barracks in Licka Jesenica, which was behind our backs at an elevation, they opened fire on Brdina area. We didn't have proper radio communication with them, and I ordered our unit to withdraw in the -- through the area of Vukelic Poljana, so that we wouldn't suffer losses from friendly fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to illustrate this combat, you said that the 5th Partisan Brigade was supposed to leave from the direction of Kuselj. Looking at the asphalt road leading to Titova Korenica, as one leaves that road, can you tell us what settlements there are?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Going from Korenica, one has to cross the Korenica bridge first and then one turns left. The first village one comes across is Poljanak, and then Sertic Poljana, and then there is a forest, and then one comes out to a clearing where Kuselj begins. Following Kuselj, there is the area we called Saborsko, and then Funtana, and then Saborsko itself. And then one comes to a slope going down Borik, and this is where Licka Jesenica begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So according to this JNA plan, the 5th Partisan Brigade was to start out from Kuselj and meet up with you, going in the direction of Licka Jesenica. Did I portray it properly?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did. However, they had this forest, this narrow road which was completely blocked by trees, tall trees, and it was not a passable road. Those trees needed to be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. -- sir, you just said that they had a forest. Who had that forest and who had that blocked road?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: The direction from which the 5th Partisan Brigade was supposed to advance we called them the unit from Korenica. They were coming from Korenica, and they were supposed to link up with us approximately halfway between Brdina and Jelen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So this 5th Partisan Brigade came across a blocked road. It was blocked with tree-trunks and they were unable to proceed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, they did not carry out their mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you went from the opposite direction, from Licka Jesenica towards Saborsko, and when you came across fortified positions you withdrew because you came under friendly fire, the fire of the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. During the attack, the tank unit was in the centre progressing along the asphalt road. One tank went to attack the barracks in Licka Jesenica, together with Commander Bulat in order to provide support to us, because, from there, they would have better visibility. They were some 45 kilometres away as the crow flies, which is the range of attack, and it was precisely that tank that opened friendly fire against us. They were unable to see us. We didn't have radio communication with them, and this is how this came to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Saborsko well? Are you familiar with Saborsko as a village? Can one say you know where the major buildings are, the school, the churches and so on?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, one might say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How many churches were there in Saborsko at the time of that attack?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: In Saborsko itself, there was one large church in the middle of the village. It was a Catholic church and it stood on a small elevation. Looking from the direction of Licka Jesenica to the right of the road, next to the cemetery, there was a small church. I think it was a stone church.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you described this little church, the stone church, which as you say could be seen from the Licka Jesenica barracks, where were these fortified positions you came across, in relation to that church?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: They were in its immediate vicinity, and I also saw the air force active in that area. I think that area was bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, when you say "immediate vicinity," that's very relative. Can you be more precise? Can you tell us in hundreds or dozens of metres, because this is very vague.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a good commander will never put a firing position near a church, because its position is clearly marked in all topographic maps and it is easy to target with that artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the question you are being asked. You are being asked: Give us the distance in metres, please, just listen to the questions and answer the questions. Don't tell us about a good or a bad commander. Tell us the distance. What do you mean by "immediate vicinity?" How many metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more than 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's enough. Thank you. Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this little stone church was damaged in these military operations?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that it was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the reason why this happened and the circumstances, who did this, was responsible?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I spoke about artillery preparation. I spoke about air bombings, and this was not just one trench. It was a line of defence at a distance of some 50 metres from the church. If one is shooting from the military training ground, which is more than 10 kilometres away, the whole area was targeted by artillery fire. It could very likely have been hit by 130-millimetre guns and by mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please answer the question that was put to you now. The question that was put to you is: Do you know the reason why this happened and the circumstances, who did this? Yes or no, the reason, the circumstances were the following, this is the person who did it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour I am testifying under oath here, and I cannot say that I am certain that it was the 130-millimetre gun that damaged the church as I didn't see that. But this little church was a military position we were all firing at because they were using it as an observation post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's why the question says: Do you know? And if you don't know, you just say "I don't know." Please answer the question directly. Don't go around the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know it was hit by artillery. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the simplest answer to give. There were several questions there. The question was: Do you know the reason why it was hit and the circumstances under which it was hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason was that this area was used as an observation point, because there was an excellent view of the barracks from that position, precisely from that little church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know who did it? Who hit it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't be certain. I don't know what the -- who were the crews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, those three questions you put in one sentence. If you take them one by one, you are likely to get a more direct answer to the question and you will finish quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that at one point you ordered your unit to withdraw in order to avoid friendly fire. Did you enter Saborsko with your unit on that day, when there was fighting in and around Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether any other units entered Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: On our return to our starting positions, on securing the line in the hamlet of Vukelic Poljana, which is a Serbian hamlet and it is the closest one to Saborsko, I came to the asphalt road underneath Borik where the junction is for Vukelic Poljana, and that was when the action was practically over. At that point a group of civilians came up, led by one of our territorials who had a semi-automatic rifle slung over his shoulder. He was a man of low stature, and I think his name was Sveto or Sreto. He originates from Licka Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What you told us, what does this mean? Does this mean that the action in Saborsko, the fighting around Saborsko was already over or was the fighting still going on?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: The fighting was over by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Another question. When you and your unit entered fighting, how long did you spend in action before your withdrawing?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: If we calculate that we started out at around 9.00 a.m. and needed about two hours to get there, the fighting went on from 11.00 until 2.00 p.m. at the most. After that, we withdrew. It was not a route. It was a proper withdrawal, and it lasted two hours again. And I know because I reached that junction just as it was getting dark. It was winter and it was slowly getting dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What time might have been? It was twilight in winter.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Between 4.00 and 5.00. If I may be allowed to say so, I never carried a watch when I went into combat because it would bother me, so I can't tell you exactly what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what units entered Saborsko and when they returned and what happened subsequently?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that when we received orders to attack, we were divided into three companies, and three axes of attack. Rade Jaksic [phoen] was in command of one company, Djuro Ogrizovic [phoen] was in the centre, and I was to the right. There was also an armoured company in the centre. I think it had more than 10 tanks and some personnel carriers. The left-hand side went in front of Sivnik, which is an elevation, and the centre went along the asphalt road, and I went next to Borik hill. That was my axes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any orders to end the attack? How did all this end? You received an order to start on such and such a day at such and such a time. What about the end? Can you describe that briefly?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: In the order to attack, there was a time when the action was supposed to end, but no one can predict the end of the operation exactly. But I saw the tanks going back before nightfall, and night falls at around 6.00 p.m. at that time of year. I didn't have good communications or any communications, in fact, because my hand-held radio set broke down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to the civilian population in Saborsko? You told us a little while ago that you saw a man with a group of civilians from Saborsko. Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: The group I saw and talked to went to the school in Licka Jesenica, which is about one kilometre, or two at the most, from the spot where we met. The same man who was leading them escorted them there. I didn't know all the people from Saborsko, but in that group I recognised a Serb, because there were two or three Serb houses in Saborsko. Their last name was Salaja [phoen]. In the meantime he had grown a moustache, so I didn't recognise him right away. I only recognised him when I approached him. They left and they were received by the TO from Licka Jesenica. I know that well. They were put up in the school, provided with a cooked meal. There was no electricity, but they were given some kind of lamp, and they were told they need not be afraid and that they were completely safe there. On the following day, I visited that group in civilian clothes. I went to that school and I spoke to them. They said they wanted to go to the Croatian side, and they were taken in buses from Licka Jesenica to the Croatian side. I told them to wait one day just in case there were other people in the woods, because they couldn't live in Saborsko any longer because the conditions there were not right, so we should wait. If any more people turned up, they could all be taken to the Croatian side together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So did they go to the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were some 20 men and women; mostly elderly men in that group. Afterwards, I heard from Dusan Latas, who was the police commander. I heard from him first-hand that there was a group which was late, and he took them in the official police car, three or four people who missed the bus. I don't know what the total number of civilians is that was taken to the area between Josipdol and Vojinovac, but I think at least 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, do you know how inhabitants lived in Saborsko, for example in early 1990, approximately?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think about a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned some 30 people who expressed a wish after the fighting to go over to the Croatian side. Do you know what happened to the remaining population of Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: During the attack, probably intentionally, but I never discussed it with the late Mr. Bulat, an axis was left open from Saborsko towards Slunj. Nobody covered it and it was not used for attack. Most likely it was meant to be a route for civilians to withdraw. I don't know because I didn't discuss it, but I assume that's what it was, and I assume that most of the population of Saborsko used that axis to go towards Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether there were any victims in Saborsko? When I say "victims," I mean on the Croatian side as it was a Croatian village, and you said that only a few people in the hamlet of Salaja were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know about those three. They were soldiers, and I know because later on I passed through Saborsko, after the lifting of the blockade, and I know that there were civilian casualties. I even issued an order, as it was within my area of responsibility, to sanitize the terrain. It wasn't just that there were human corpses; there were carcasses of cattle. So the terrain had to be sanitized, cattle and livestock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to guesstimate the number of civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need to guess, because I received a report of the sanitization of the terrain. The civilian protection staff delivered a report to me. It was on my desk in the municipality. I can't remember the exact number, though. But I think it was more than 20. They were buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to the issue of sanitization a bit later. There's one thing I'm interested in. The JNA was in command of the operation and the fighting around Saborsko. And when the units withdrew from the village, was a unit left to secure the village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A platoon commanded by Savator Bojavic [phoen] was left there. We refer to him as Sava Crni, or Sava The Black. They remained there to secure the terrain around the village of Dumancici [phoen], which is below Borik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And did they carry out this order? Have you any knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my knowledge is precisely the opposite. I think they had clear orders as to what they were supposed to do and what they were supposed to prevent, but I'm afraid they did quite the opposite. I wasn't there that evening, or the following day, so I can't speak at first hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me interrupt you. You said you knew what the orders were and what they were supposed to prevent. So tell us what were the orders and what was it that they were supposed to prevent?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were supposed to prevent people who had not participated in the action, because I have to say that every army, including ours, had a component which did not participate in combat, but rather engaged in looting and burning, and when those who were fighting and risking their lives had done their job, they would be followed by such people, such petty thieves who would perpetrate bad things. So the orders were to secure the area, to prevent such people from entering it. However, unfortunately, such things did happen after the operation was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that as president of the municipality, if I understand you correctly, you gave the order for the terrain to be sanitized. To whom did you give this order? Who carried this out, and when?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Following the conclusion of that operation, we first had to clear the road of the tree-trunks that were an obstacle to the 5th Partisan Brigade that I already described in order to make the road passable. In the meantime, an order had come from Belgrade to establish a JNA brigade in Plaski, for the TO brigade to be transformed into the JNA brigade, and the new commander had arrived, Petar Trbovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let us clarify this first. You said that an order had arrived from Belgrade. What do you mean? Who issued that order to establish a JNA brigade with Petar Trbovic? Which organ issued that order?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time it was only in the jurisdiction of the federal secretariat for national defence, because at the time this was still within the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Continue.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: So Colonel Trbovic came, bringing with him a command of active officers, over 20 of them, all issued with tasks, and in keeping with their military specialty they were given special assignments. And there was a company in Jesenica comprising people who resided there, and then there was a company in Janja Gora and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I understand that. You are now speaking of the TO brigade in Plaski.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to draw a distinction between that brigade and the JNA brigade which was later established. So the JNA brigade was established bearing in mind military occupational specialty. Within the SFRY, every male who had served in the army had his military occupational specialty and, as such, he performed certain roles and special -- or, rather, in certain units. People had their military booklets, and units were established in accordance with military occupational specialties, and this brigade that was established was called 145th Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. When was it established in relation to the Saborsko events?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: 10 days after that, at the most. Why am I saying this? Because in the meantime there was also an operation in Slunj carried out, after the fall of Saborsko. The events progressed very fast. There were basically daily operations from Josipdol and other areas. Most likely they had their units remaining in the woods, and they engaged our forces. This is just my assumption. So some of the units were engaged in the attack on Slunj, and out of the remaining ones we had no one to leave in Saborsko and to begin this task that remained to be done, which was to collect the war booty and to carry out the sanitization of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you said this operation Saborsko was concluded on the same day it began?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Then you said the operation towards Slunj continued. Who led it, and what do you mean "towards Slunj." Who was in charge of that operation?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: Tactical Group 2 once again received an order; I think that the order was for one company from our brigade to participate in it. It was either on the 16th or on the 17th, just five days after Saborsko. And when you pull out a company from a brigade, that is to say you pull out 100 men out of 1.000 men, you can feel this loss. You can feel that these people are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There was a reference to "collection of war booty." What actually was collected by way of booty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the unit which had come from Zagreb brought with them mortars, recoilless, a recoilless gun, anti-aircraft guns, so whatever they were unable to take with them, that is to say heavy weapons, in order to prevent the weapons from falling into the enemy hands. So that was one goal. And then the other goal was to collect the cattle that had gone wandering, in order for the cattle to be used to feed the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know how many cattle were collected to feed the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that the cattle was brought to Plaski and that there were more than 50 cattle head. Mostly cows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we're on the question of cattle, you referred earlier to carcasses of cattle that were also killed during the combat. Are you able to tell us how many were killed during the combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Saborsko was a village, and every household had cattle or at least they had pigs and poultry, and most people had cows and some sheep. That is to say, that the cattle was used to being fed by people. Pigs especially can carry on without human presence only for a brief period of time. Some were killed by artillery fire, and some just died on their own, because they were shut in the barns. So I didn't go myself into the barns, but just passing on the road I could see that, and I wanted to find who was responsible for that. And we found a manual for civilian protection, and we saw that this was something that the civilian protection staff should do. So I issued an order to them to do that. And there was a danger that there would be an epidemic, that there would be an infection breaking out. So I carried out -- so I issued an order for this to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please, now, answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked me how many head of cattle died? It's hard for me to say how many, but all I can tell you is that there were many. Not less than 100, including pigs and bovine, cattle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now that we have opened up this topic, you said that you issued an order to the civilian protection team to carry out the sanitization of the terrain. Did this civilian protection team have any obligation in regard to any human victims?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: A change occurred at the time. I remember that this involved mostly the elderly who were not active in the brigade. I remember the name of Nikola Kordic. Previously I had appointed him chief of civilian protection staff, and since he was of poor health he was soon replaced by Milan Susnjar, who was also over 60. They established an ad hoc unit comprising people who were not members of the brigade. I remember that my neighbour, Ozran Popovic, who was a male nurse, was one of the members. And then I also remember Djura, who was a forester. Mostly elderly from Plaski were members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they have any equipment they needed to carry out this task, and what about human victims?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC
utterances.text: We had no equipment whatsoever. But we spoke to Commander Trbovic and arranged that a loader be provided to them, so that they can dig graves, and this was implemented. Later on I received a report, and I remember this report well. Based on it, this was done on several occasions, two or three times, because one needs quite a lot of time to travel from Saborsko to Plaski, and it was winter-time. And an order was issued for a human corpses to be buried as close as possible to the place where they fell victim and also not -- to bury them with everything found on them, including any ID, so that later on, the exchange of corpses can be carried out. And later on we did precisely that. We exchanged all the corpses and all of the prisoners who had been taken prisoner during the war. So the order was not to bury corpses and carcasses together under any circumstances. All sites containing human remains were to be marked by a cross and, as I said, they were supposed to be buried as close as possible to the place where they died, so that this information could be used in the process of identification. I read the report, and I was able to see that the order was closely followed. There was something I didn't like in that report. For example, they said that there were three members of MUP buried, and I didn't like the fact how they described these people. They assured me, however, that everything was done in accordance with international law, and that I was able to see that for myself.
